# Notes on Joshua 20 (Cities of Refuge), verse by verse

**What I couldn't find:** I didn't find anything specific to this chapter from Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox teachers, or from the debated modern movements (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace). So those are left out. Enduring Word is listed under Pentecostal/charismatic in your site list, but I treat David Guzik below as a general evangelical voice, because his page doesn't speak for that tradition. Most of the Protestant disagreement I found falls on v. 6.

---

**v. 1**
- Keil and Delitzsch say the six towns were set apart after the land was shared out, following Moses' instructions in Numbers 35. After the distribution of the land by lot among the tribes of Israel, six towns were set apart, in accordance with the Mosaic instructions in Numbers 35, as places of refuge for unintentional manslayers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/20-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Calvin's editor says he stood almost alone in reading this command as an indirect censure of the Israelites, for not having previously of their own accord appointed cities of refuge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/20-1.html
- **The opposite view:** a note on Precept Austin says the command doesn't mean Joshua was failing in his duty. No delinquency on the part of Joshua is to be inferred from this command. Others on the Calvin page think the timing was simply right, because every city of refuge had to be a Levite city, so they couldn't be chosen until the Levites had theirs. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-20-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/20-1.html
- **Modern scholarship and the Catholic Encyclopedia:** both are reported as dating the cities late.
  - Coffman describes a critical view that the cities began only after Josiah's reforms in 621 BC. Before that, on this view, a killer took refuge at the local altar (Exodus 21:14). 
  - Coffman, a conservative, calls this view false and points to Abner's death at Hebron (2 Samuel 3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/joshua-20.html
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia suggests the three western cities were probably established in the time of Josias, and that the eastern three were added after the Exile. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12712a.htm

**v. 2**
- God gave this command first through Moses, in Numbers 35:9–34 and Deuteronomy 19:1–13. Referring back to Moses also backs up Joshua's leadership. https://biblehub.com/joshua/20-2.htm
- The Hebrew word for "refuge" (*miqlat*) is always used of these asylum cities. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62612/
- **Wesley (Methodist):** the cities were designed to typify the relief which the gospel provides for poor, penitent sinners. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html
- **Matthew Henry:** God would not have given these cities so much attention in the law unless they were meant to picture the gospel's refuge in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/20.htm
- **A dissenting older view:** an author quoted on Bible Hub says the cities have no typical meaning, though they may illustrate Christian truth. In his view, God allowed the custom of blood revenge while also restraining it, because Israel was not ready for it to be abolished. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/20-1.htm

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** the cities protected someone guilty of manslaughter but not of murder. The "avenger of blood" (Hebrew *goel*) was the family member responsible for seeing justice done. He also quotes Howard, who says the avenger had legal standing and was not taking private revenge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-20/
- **Wesley:** the text says "unawares" and "unwittingly" twice so that wilful murderers would have no hope of protection. Wesley also criticises Christians whose church sanctuaries sheltered such people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html
- **Whedon (Methodist):** the city was there to give anyone accused a chance to show he had no guilty intent. That meant the guilty also had to be taken in for a time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-20.html

**v. 4**
- **The gate:** the court sat at the city gate (Whedon). Wesley says the judges sat there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-20.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html
- Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say the elders had to give the man shelter and a living until the proper authorities had looked into the case. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jos/Jos_020.cfm
- Guzik quotes Madvig: a person was treated as innocent until proven guilty, and at least two witnesses were needed to convict him (Numbers 35:30). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-20/

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** the elders had to protect the man who fled to them. The case shows that Israel's law weighed intent and premeditation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-20/
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** the deliberate murderer, once found guilty, was shut out from any shelter and could not be ransomed. The author uses this to argue against abolishing capital punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-20.html

**v. 6 (where Protestant teachers differ most)**
- **Who judged?**
  - Poole and Wesley say "the congregation" was the court of the killer's home town, not the elders of the refuge city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/20-6.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html
  - Coffman takes it as the assembly of the refuge city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/20-6.html
- **Was the stay a punishment?**
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says yes: manslaughter was severely punished. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-20.html
  - Utley (quoted on bible.org) says the man paid a price by being cut off from his home. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-20
  - Trapp says the exile was because there had been some carelessness on the killer's part. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/joshua-20.html
- **Why the high priest's death? Several competing views:**
  - *It pictures Christ's death.* Keil, and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, link it to the priest being anointed with holy oil, and see his death as a type of the heavenly High Priest's death (Hebrews 9:14–15). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jos/Jos_020.cfm
  - *It is not a type of Christ.* The Pulpit Commentary rejects this outright. It says the high priest's ordinary death could not atone for anything, and that it was his yearly entry into the holy place on the Day of Atonement that pictured Christ. It prefers Bähr's idea, supported by Maimonides: the high priest stood for the whole nation, so his death was a national grief in which private grievances were set aside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/20-6.htm
  - *He carried the people's guilt.* Ellicott argues that the high priest, as the nation's representative, bore the guilt, and his death released it. So he calls the familiar saying "Our High Priest can never die," is beside the mark. The point, he says, is that Christ *has* died. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-20.html
  - *Christ's eternal priesthood is the comfort.* This is the very idea Ellicott pushes against. Redpath (quoted by Guzik) rests the believer's safety on a High Priest who "lives forever." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-20/
  - *It refers to the end of the age (Brethren, dispensational).* William Kelly reads it as being about the future: when Christ ends his heavenly priesthood, "all Israel" will be brought back to their land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/20-6.html
  - *It is too fanciful.* Blaikie mentions the "mystical meaning" some find here, then stresses how Christ's protection goes beyond it. https://ccel.org/ccel/blaikie/expositorjosh/expositorjosh.xxviii.html
- **What the picture says about the security of salvation (applications differ):**
  - Guzik draws a parallel: protection held only inside the city, and going outside meant death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-20/
  - On Precept Austin, the opposite point is made, apparently by Wiersbe (the page doesn't say clearly who wrote it): the fugitive could be killed if he left too soon, but our salvation in Christ is not conditional. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-20-commentary

**v. 7**
- **"Set apart":** the Hebrew means "sanctified." Henry says this was a public legal declaration, not a ceremony. Whedon says it marked the cities as surrounded by God's special mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/20.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/joshua-20.html
- **Levite cities:**
  - Wesley gives two reasons: Levites would judge fairly, and their standing would hold back people bent on revenge. He adds that the refugee, unable to go to the sanctuary, had God's servants nearby to teach him and pray for him. Henry says much the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html
  - A note on Precept Austin says Levite cities and cities of refuge were not the same thing: only 6 of the 48 Levite cities gave asylum. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62613/
- **Where they stood (the sources disagree):**
  - Wesley says the cities were on mountains, so they could be seen from far off.
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary quotes a traveller who calls that idea a mistake, at least for Kedesh, which is hidden under a mountain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-20.html
- **Meanings of the names:**
  - Henry suggests Kedesh = holy, Shechem = shoulder and Hebron = fellowship, while saying he takes no pleasure in "quibbling upon names." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/20.htm
  - Moody and Adrian Rogers (Baptist) build sermons on these meanings. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-20-commentary

**v. 8**
- Moses had already named these three eastern cities (Deuteronomy 4:41). Wesley reads the verse as "had assigned." Henry cites Bishop Patrick's view that the cities had not received their rights until now. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/20.htm
- The western and eastern cities roughly faced each other, so no one was far from safety. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/20-1.htm

**v. 9**
- **Who were the "foreigners"?** Wesley says not only converts to Israel's faith but others too, because this was a matter of common right. Trapp leaves open whether it meant all foreigners or converts only. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-20.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/joshua-20.html
- Guzik says God's justice applied to everyone without favour. He also notes one key contrast with Christ: the cities sheltered only the innocent, while the guilty can come to Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-20/
- **Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship):** the cities gave asylum until the elders could judge the case, and someone found not guilty of murder could go on living there. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/refuge/
- **Coffman:** the cities are an emblem of the Church, which is open to more than those who sinned unknowingly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/joshua-20.html
